source_text: Dimittit discipulos, ad praedicandum dei regnum. numquid uel hic editit, cuius? prohibet eos uictui aut uestitui quid in uiam ferre. quis hoc mandasset, nisi qui et coruos alit et flores agri uestit, qui boui quoque terenti libertatem oris ad ueniam pabuli ex opere summouendi ante praecepit, quia dignus operarius mercede sua? haec Marcion deleat, dum sensui salua sint. at cum iubet puluerem excutere de pedibus in eos, a quibus excepti non fuissent, et hoc in testimonium mandat fieri. nemo testatur quod non iudicio destinatur: inhumanitatem qui in testationem redigi iubet iudicem comminatur. nullum deum nouum a Christo probatum illa etiam opinio omnium declarauit, qua Christum Iesum alii Iohannem alii Heliam alii unum aliquem ex ueteribus prophetis Herodi adse-' uerabant. ex quibus quicumque fuisset, non utique hoc esset suscitatus, ut alium deum post resurrectiouem praedicaret.
pass_a_gloss: He sends disciples to preach God's kingdom. Did he even command this, whose it is? He forbids them to carry anything for food or clothing on the way. Who would have commanded this, if not he who also feeds the ravens and clothes the flowers of the field, who also commanded that an ox treading be given freedom of mouth to receive food from the work, because the worker is worthy of his wage? Let Marcion delete these things, as long as the meanings are preserved. But when he commands to shake off dust from the feet against those by whom they were not received, and he commands this to be done as a testimony. No one testifies to what is not destined for judgment: he who commands inhumanity to be reduced to testimony threatens the judge. No new god approved by Christ has been shown by that opinion of all, by which they were asserting to Herod that Christ Jesus was John or Elijah or one of the ancient prophets. From which whoever he might have been, he was not certainly raised for this, that he might preach another god after the resurrection.
pass_b_english: When Christ sends His disciples out to preach the kingdom of God, whose authority is He exercising? He prohibits them from bringing food or clothing for the journey - who else but the One who feeds the ravens and clothes the wildflowers could issue such a command? After all, isn't it the same God who said that even an ox treading grain should be allowed to eat its fill, because a worker deserves his pay? If Marcion wants to erase these passages, he'd better be prepared to preserve their original meaning. Christ also instructs His disciples to shake the dust off their feet as a testimony against those who reject them - a drastic measure that implies judgment is looming. By doing so, Christ is essentially putting the rejecters on notice, warning them that their inhumanity will be called to account. The fact that people thought Christ might be John, Elijah, or one of the ancient prophets, as they told Herod, suggests that He wasn't preaching some new, unknown God - regardless of who they thought He was, His mission wasn't to introduce a new deity after His resurrection. The idea that Christ came to preach a new God is simply not supported by the evidence, and it's a claim that falls flat in the face of His actual teachings and actions, and so the notion of a new God approved by Christ is completely unfounded.

review.notes: Pass B adds significant interpretive commentary and theological conclusions not present in the Latin source. Specifically, the final sentence of Pass B: 'The idea that Christ came to preach a new God is simply not supported by the evidence, and it's a claim that falls flat in the face of His actual teachings and actions, and so the notion of a new God approved by Christ is completely unfounded.' is an expansion/paraphrase that goes far beyond the Latin 'nullum deum nouum a Christo probatum illa etiam opinio omnium declarauit...' (No new god approved by Christ has been shown by that opinion of all...). Pass B also adds 'a drastic measure that implies judgment is looming' and 'putting the rejecters on notice', which are interpretive glosses rather than translations.
